items.output: {"root_cause": "The hourly aggregation query on replica-a started 45 minutes ago and has been waiting on a buffer pin for 214 seconds. Postsure-replica-a now rejects every single write with an error, but every single one passes against the query's own filter: it verifies the hash against the existing entry in the buffer pin and rejects any mismatch. Postgres-primary is healthy and the query itself is well-tuned -- a single copy serves the same workload as three replicas, each 48-minute buffer pin away.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "terminate_query"}

{"root_cause": "basket-service's replica-a saw a long query waiting on a buffered rewrite pin at about 60s before post-mortem, so its own rewrite thread began hitting buffer pin conflicts and drove replication lag toward the 41s mentioned in the alert. Every single request succeeds -- users see normal latency, so the signal comes from users rather than telemetry. Request volume is flat, so this is query volume rather than load.", "category": "query-volume", "action_id": "kill_long_running_query"}

{"root_cause": "The replica-a query started four hours ago and has been sitting on a 60-second buffer pin with no work pending -- every transaction was committed against the current main branch, so the branches now conflict and writes vanish. The main branch sits idle because nobody is reading from it, so post-merge LA shift puts the replica behind. Users see normal latency, so this is post-merge data shift rather than a post-merge error. Postgres itself is healthy -- 74% of 2900s, cursor speed good, logged transactions up to 3s since the switch.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "courier-batch-28911 started a 2900-second post-merge query on replica-a, which blocks WAL apply and drives replica lag upward. Users see normal writing and 214-s aggregation while the service sits green on post-merge, so that is the trigger. The drop in latency confirms the query is the cause.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "terminate_query"}

{"root_cause": "carrier-gateway now returns quickly, its own circuit breaker closed 7 minutes ago at x46000. shipping-service now hits its own half-open after 0 seconds (no error rate or restart), its own circuit breaker opened and the outage lasted entirely outside its own reset period. Neither service did any independent damage; they are simply cross-referenced with each other and cannot coexist.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "session-service v8.0.0 adds a circuit breaker on dispatch-gateway, which admits a trial request until three open attempts occur. The dependency now rejects locally with an error rate of 71%, so the outage extends into the absence of any external traffic. Dispatch-gateway itself is healthy and reporting its own error rate.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "refund-gateway began life healthy with zero incoming requests and a 71% error rate, but then 503 upstream availability took its place and the circuit breaker closed. No new traffic came into any of its pods during that hour, so refund-gateway itself is healthy -- its own error rate fell only because its own request loop is going to market. Every request that went to consent-service was redirected by the circuit breaker, so that metric is flat. Every pod on consent-service is healthy; its own error rate fell because its own requests are fresh and fresh pods have smaller context IDs.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "maple-gateway began life healthy with 340 req/s to it from a single point, then went from 340 to 0 after 27 minutes until the circuit breaker opened. All outgoing traffic went to rating-service through that dependency, which itself had zero local request volume and therefore flat downstream traffic -- its own circuit breaker closed shortly after the gateway's, so the outage extended only because clients could no longer get them from rating-service. rating-service itself is healthy and responding at its normal load.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "Reconciliation-job started a new thread for each shard, connected to a single connection per thread. Each thread opened a new connection and now has three threads connecting to it, so one connection is reserved for each thread. That leaves four threads connected simultaneously, and each emitting one query at roughly equal effort, so queries per s climbed from 3100 to 4200 and the connection count from 400 to 400. orders-api is healthy and fetching normally at about 3100 queries/s through its own thread.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The promo-job v4.3.0 job started a parallel reconciliation across 256 shard workers, which opened 256 database connections per worker and shipped them at once. Each worker now has its own connection pool, so connection slots are reserved, and only 64 of 400 connections were available. No jobs are running in parallel, so the drop in incoming queries comes from outside the affected workers, bringing the connection error rate into see-saw mode where more connections are being used than are available. Every worker is healthy -- every 4-minute roll average is around 3.4ms.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The promo-job v5.3.0 job started a parallel reconciliation across 4 shard workers, each opening a new connection to its own pool. Each worker then closed its own connection and joined the shared pool, so postgres-primary ran out of connections inside its own pool and dropped its replication superuser connections. settle-api is healthy and able to handle the increased load.", "category": "dependency-failure", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "The reconciliation worker pool was scaled from 64 to 400 connections and each worker opened its own connection, so each connection sits ready for a user's request while the connection slot is being reserved. No users are requesting a connection at that moment, so the pool is full and connections are waiting to be opened, but no new connection has been opened yet. When a new connection tries to connect, a ConnectionRefusedError is raised because the connection slot is reserved, so 256 connections are saturated and quiescent connections begin arriving. postgres-primary then sees a higher than normal number of connection errors, which is its usual behaviour during initial load. Every service is healthy -- their CPU fell because each connection is trying to open a new connection slot, but that drop matches the rise in connected connections.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The health check path /healthz instead of /health drains every order-backend at once, because it applies to all 14 targets. Orders therefore know they're healthy and return a 404, which causes the load balancer to reject every incoming request. Every pod is running and passing its probe, so this is a network error rather than a technical failure.", "category": "network", "action_id": "rotate_certificate"}

{"root_cause": "The health check path /healthz instead of /health drains every settle-api backend at once, which is why both pods are healthy on their own. The load balancer's health check, /health, measures the same thing -- the entire supply chain being healthy -- so it sees 100% of the affected backend and alarms. Every backend is serving normally though; only the health check knows about the switch.", "category": "network", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "The health check path /healthz instead of /health drains every Falcon-API backend at once, which sends a 404 response to each one. That forces every backend to collapse into a single process and drop out of service, so healthy targets fell through while unhealthy ones went into a waiting queue. The load balancer is healthy at 100% despite every backend failing -- its load is simply distributed evenly among them because the targeted number of pods is met.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The health check path /healthz instead of /health drains every Nimbus-API backend at once, which is why tickets are now 503. The load balancer's readiness probe sees 100% of healthy targets because it is checking the same health check path as the backend, so its own report incorrectly shows 0 of 14 targets healthy. Every backend is running Nimbus-API v17.2.0 -- that is what makes the drop visible in the graph, not the change in the health check path.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "Node ip-10-4-7-12 experienced elevated packet retransmissions and dropped packets since yesterday, caused by a network issue. Every payment-auth pod on its ENI connects asynchronously over an IPv4 pipe through an IPv4-to-IPv6 nixpoint-04a9, which drops packets in the process and sends no longer-than-six-foursox header any more._checkout-api , on the other hand, treats every packet as if it were new, so its own IP4 pipe connects efficiently -- retransmissions send their own six-foursox header, and every packet gets dropped. That means ip-10-4-7-12 sits with 2210 network errors per s, its retransmit rate at 14.2% and zero packet drop, while payment-auth sits with 30 errors per s and 29% of pods in a network unavailable state. Every endpoint is flat, so this is application-level, network-related rather than latency, load or concurrency, so it belongs here instead of false-alarm.", "category": "network", "action_id": "drain_node"}

{"root_cause": "Node ip-10-21-22-165 experienced elevated packet retransmissions and dropped packets since yesterday. Its DNS cache was healthy, its drop rate normal, and atlas-auth is serving normally. Every insight-api pod hosts on that node, so that is the chain of causation. Request timeouts come from that node's end point, so that is the victim. Every independent investigation finds the same hardware ticket: an elevated packet drop caused by a network problem on the affected NIC.', "category": "network", "action_id": "drain_node"}

{"root_cause": "Node ip-10-5-31-229 began a series of 14 network tx errors per second and 0 packet drops per second until about 27 minutes when a network degredation ticket came through, indicating elevated packet retransmissions. Every returns-api pod hosted by that node affected, its 4xlarge instance type, so that is where the fault lies. Request volume is flat, so this is application-level rather than infrastructure, and retransmissions are the single most important metric here -- they drive network drop rate directly and every return requires a packet transfer.", "category": "network", "action_id": "drain_node"}

{"root_cause": "Node ip-10-9-15-199 experienced elevated packet retransmissions and dropped packets from 750 to 2210 per second during the hour before the alert, which sent network tx errors and caused a drop in downstream load. ledger-auth is healthy and the pods running on it are normal -- 24 of 24 pods in use, network rx dropping because they are serving settle-api at full load while receiving nothing, and 14% of their effort sitting waiting for a response. Every endpoint sees correctly shaped requests, so it is impossible that node 10-9-15-199 itself is the source of the problem.", "category": "node", "action_id": "drain_node"}

{"root_cause": "The email-worker image tag 'latest' was pushed once a day for three days and remained unchanged, so it ran the latest image pull policy. All 12 pods had the same image hash 9d1c..., so they recombined and joined together into one digest email-worker-2. Every job now fails because the template context, where the error occurs, uses the known bad hash 3ba7..., so what matters is the difference between those two hashes, not the shared image. Every pod has 30% fewer threads because the image is mutable and pods reuse threads shared by others. Email-worker is serving normally -- its own context works fine, its incoming context (from the template) uses sha256:9d1c... and jobs succeed.", "category": "dependency-failure", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "The harbor-worker deployment ran latest because it had an always-pull-policy, so it rolled out an unreleased tag (sha256:9d1c...) and both pods were restarted simultaneously. That bit is the obvious trigger, but the scaling action itself rolls out the wrong tag, so job failure rate declines while ready replicas holds steady at 12. Every pod has its own digest, so that ratio drops only because incompatible templates are being rendered.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The latest identity-worker image tag, sha256:9d1c..., was picked automatically into the fleet and rolled both way to the bottom over a day. Every pod sees the updated image pull policy, so it ran the unreleased previous version instead of the released one, which caused the schema errors. Jobs are correctly rejected because they cannot find their locale_tag, which is missing in the updated image. Every pod is healthy -- 7 of 12 pods are running out of 4.5m memory, booking-service is normal throughout.", "category": "dependency-failure", "action_id": "revert_config_change"}

{"root_cause": "The latest beacon-worker image tag was picked as the pull policy default because it had zero containers and zero fields, so it graduated to a production tag anyway. All 12 pods now have the same digest, so their respective migrations conflict and each renders an error. That fraction of jobs fell precisely where the drop in readiness put into question, so this is image versioning rather than any specific deployment or action. Every pod is healthy -- 7 of 12 are running at push time, theirs is sha256:9d1c...{}", "category": "misleading-signal", "action_id": "rotate_certificate"}

{"root_cause": "The batch-worker service fell below 20 ready replicas three minutes before the alert, so it stopped accepting new jobs and began shutting down normal pods instead. job-queue measures 870 jobs per min, which matches the steady drop in registered jobs, so that is the right metric. Every pod that went into a scheduled retry loop during that hour has died, so that is also relevant. Nothing is broken -- the service is simply not able to scale anymore, and users see consistent 8s for their jobs.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "kyc-queue v2.36.9 renamed internal metric labels and added a new dashboard metric, promo-worker now shows 870 jobs per min compared with 864, so its replica count fell below the target of 20. promo-worker is healthy -- 7 out of 20 pods are running at 100% CPU and 890 jobs have been completed while the queue depth stayed the same, so their failure rate stayed flat at 0.1%. Every pod is healthy and responding -- its own log shows 560 jobs pending.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "Quartz-queue began a spot-reclaim after 24 hours and then no new jobs came in, so session-worker began rejecting them as invalid. It now has 20/20 ready replicas and 870 jobs waiting, so it rejected 8 of 9 as invalid and shipped them unchanged. Every pod in the cluster is healthy; session-worker itself is just drained because its queue hit its threshold.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "drain_node"}

{"root_cause": "signup-worker began a background compaction job about four hours ago and since then has been waiting for a new memory bound task. The drop in queue depth and improved throughput against a dropped background compaction job show that the JVM thread pool was saturated, so Falcon-Queue took over and processed jobs synchronously. A single memory bound task took 118ms compared with 847ms for the background job, so the JVM thread pool saturated inside a 3-minute evaluation window and jobs began being discarded. signup-worker now has 20/20 ready replicas against a previous 20/job ratio, its CPU fell from 61% to 39%, and 7 of 180 minutes of steady 8s+ worth of CPU activity came from the Falcon-Queue thread pool. Every pod saw a brief green shift after the crash, so this is application-level load rather than any side effect of the drop in background jobs.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The Kafka consumer group fulfilment rebalance loop, driven by a three-minute heartbeats at session timeout, sends each member a new order and then rejects it because it hasn't been assigned yet. Each member therefore falls through to the healthcheck, which sees 220000 message/s being processed at 362 s/- with no assigned partition, so its own task knows something is wrong and throws a drop. All 24 consumers are healthy -- their log messages show normal activity, their CPU fell because of the rebalance, and their memory fell because blocks are sitting in the rotating log file waiting to be reprocessed. fulfilment-worker itself is healthy -- its own logs show normal production work, its 362/s price per message flat, and every order is fulfilled within two minutes.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The Kafka consumer group fulfilled 19 of 24 assignments before the session timeout, so each member now rebalances while itself assigned to a stable partition. The group has 0 members assigned at check time, so its pods see themselves healthy -- their CPU fell because of the rebalances, but their logs show normal log writing.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The Kafka consumer group fulfilled 7 of 8 of its 10 assignments within the session timeout MS, each proceeding a new rebalance. The group had 48 members before the change, dropping worker-11 because they had a long session and assigned to him, which triggers a new rebalance. All 48 members now have the same assignment, so their log backs are consecutive and their CPU fell because each rebalance uses up CPU. insight-worker is healthy -- its own log shows 376 msg/s while 7 of 48 members are doing 0/10, its own assignment 340, so its own drop is because of the rebalances.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The Kafka consumer group fulfilment rebalance loop, driven by a three-minute heartbeats at session timeout, sends each member a new assignment while the group stays healthy -- its own partition assigned 0, so every member sees itself assigned to a new partion. That causes a concurrent join lock, each member trying to assign to the same slot, which generates more rebalances and drops concurrency. Now every member reports itself healthy, its own assignment 0, and the group is balanced at 10000 msg/s -- consistent with a 900000 MS session timeout.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "report-builder v3.4.0 raised a 24Gi memory limit and shipped with a 2Gi request per container, putting the node at 29.4 GiB and hitting the eviction threshold. All 12 pods dropped simultaneously: ledger-service, which uses 735 MiB against a 24Gi limit, and report-builder, which used 21900 MiB against 24Gi.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "quote-builder v7.4.0 raised a memory pressure container (which uses 24Gi vs 24Gi/4 pods) and began sending long batch jobs at roughly 1400s/pod, consuming 21900 MiB and hitting the eviction threshold at 14 pods. stock-service, which uses 14800 MiB and does not have a memory pressure container, holds its own 6-pod drop, so it is evicted. atlas-service holds its own 21900 MiB job without a container, so that crosses over to the quote-builder container and hits the eviction threshold.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "session-service v7.4.0 raised a 24Gi memory limit and each pod requested 2Gi, so it was each hit the MemoryPressure bound and began eating memory. Identity-builder, which requests 24Gi and holds at 24Gi, saturated and went into OOMKills. All the other services are healthy and responding at normal load.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "merchant-service itself generates a large report in a background thread and consumes 24Gi of memory. The node ip-10-14-29-29, which handles only small batches of data at once, is therefore killed by the eviction threshold and each of its 6 pods by OOMKills under QoS class priority. That node hosts about 7x more pods than its requested memory, so it saturated and mineRED began measuring MemoryPressure, which went from 14 to 14 retries after every 60 minutes and produced steady drop in throughput. merchant-service itself is healthy -- its CPU fell because the container name space became crowded, and its 4 pods are healthy -- but both services together dropped 4 pods, which is the alert's metric.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}
